name: budget
title: A web page of your budget, with expenses by theme
pitch: Track where your money goes, on a page in your browser that only you can see. It's the biggest of the three Python projects: it mixes Python, files, HTML, forms and a small web server. The first steps don't even need the web, and a beginner who stops at step 5 already has a useful program.

steps.do: Without any web yet: write a program that asks for an expense (an amount, a theme like "food" or "rent", a short note) and prints it.
steps.done: you type an expense and see it printed back.
steps.hint: `input()` reads what you type, as text. `float()` turns "12.50" into a number.
steps.why: Start with the core of the program, in the simplest place: the terminal. The web page comes later, around something that already works.

steps.do: Keep several expenses in a list and print the total.
steps.done: three expenses give the right total.
steps.hint: A list of dictionaries works well: `{"amount": 12.5, "theme": "food", "note": "bread"}`. `sum()` adds numbers.
steps.why: Choosing how to store your data is the most important decision in a program. A list of dictionaries is simple, and it will turn into a file and a web table without changing shape.

steps.do: Save the expenses to a file (CSV or JSON) and load them when the program starts.
steps.done: you close the program, open it again, and your expenses are still there.
steps.hint: The json module: `json.dump` writes your list, `json.load` reads it back. Think about the very first run, when the file doesn't exist yet.
steps.why: A program's memory disappears when it stops. Saving to a file is how programs remember, and JSON keeps your list of dictionaries exactly as it is.

steps.do: Print the total for each theme.
steps.done: food and rent each show their own total.
steps.hint: A dictionary from theme to total: add each expense's amount to its theme's entry.
steps.why: Grouping and adding up is what turns a list of facts into an answer ("where does my money go?"). You'll use this pattern everywhere.

steps.do: Handle bad input: a word instead of a number, a negative amount, an empty theme.
steps.done: each mistake asks again instead of crashing.
steps.hint: A `while True` loop with `try` / `except ValueError` around the conversion, and `break` when the input is good.
steps.why: Never trust input, even your own. A budget with one wrong value is a wrong budget, so check data at the moment it comes in.

steps.do: Write a simple HTML page by hand (a title and a table with two fake expenses) and open it in your browser.
steps.hint: Tags you need: `<h1>`, `<table>`, `<tr>`, `<th>`, `<td>`. Open the file with your browser directly.
steps.why: Before a program writes HTML, you need to know what good HTML looks like. Writing it once by hand gives you the target.

steps.do: Make your program generate that HTML page from your saved expenses.
steps.done: after adding an expense, reloading the page shows it.
steps.hint: Build the rows with a loop and an f-string, then write the whole page to a .html file.
steps.why: Programs that write other files (HTML, reports, configs) are everywhere. This one is already a static website generator, a tiny one.

steps.do: Install Flask in a virtual environment and serve a "Hello" page on http://localhost:5000. Keep it on localhost: your budget is private.
steps.done: the browser shows "Hello" at that address.
steps.hint: Flask's quickstart has a five-line example. Don't use `host="0.0.0.0"`: that would open it to your network.
steps.why: A web server is a program that waits for requests and answers them. localhost means "this computer only": nobody else on the network can reach it.

steps.do: Serve your expenses table from Flask instead of the generated file.
steps.done: the page lists your saved expenses.
steps.hint: Load the JSON in the function of your route, and return the HTML you were already building.
steps.why: The page is now made at the moment you ask for it, so it's always up to date. That's the difference between a static page and a dynamic one.

steps.do: Add an HTML form to add an expense from the page (amount, theme, note), and save it.
steps.done: an expense added in the browser is still there after restarting the program.
steps.hint: A `<form method="post">`, a route that accepts POST, and `request.form` to read the fields. Then redirect to the page.
steps.why: A form sends data from the browser to your program. Redirecting after saving stops the browser from sending the same expense twice when you reload.

steps.do: Check the form on the server side too, like in step 5.
steps.done: a bad amount shows an error message on the page, and nothing is saved.
steps.hint: Reuse your checking code from step 5, in a function both versions can call.
steps.why: Anyone can send anything to a web server, whatever your form allows. The server must check everything itself: that's a basic rule of web security.

steps.do: Choose the theme from a list instead of typing it, and show the total per theme on the page.
steps.done: the page shows one total for each theme.
steps.hint: A `<select>` with `<option>` tags, built from your list of themes. Reuse the grouping from step 4.
steps.why: Free text gives you "Food", "food" and "fod" as three themes. A fixed list keeps your data clean, so the totals stay right.

steps.do: Add a date to each expense, and show only one month at a time.
steps.done: you can switch between two months.
steps.hint: Store dates as text like "2026-10-02": they sort correctly, and the month is the first 7 characters.
steps.why: Dates written year-month-day (ISO 8601) sort as plain text and leave no doubt about day versus month. Most programs store them this way.

steps.done: a wrong expense can be fixed from the page.
steps.hint: Give each expense an id (a number that never changes) so a link or a button can say which one.
steps.why: Data needs a stable way to be named. Positions in a list change when you delete something; ids don't.

steps.do: Optional: a monthly budget per theme with a warning when you go over it, or a chart of the themes.
steps.done: going over your food budget shows the warning.
steps.hint: Store the limits in the same JSON file, and compare them with your totals per theme.
steps.why: Now the program doesn't only show your data, it tells you something about it. That's the step from a record to a tool.
